title: School-based health center language access guide
summary: Plan school clinic language access for intake, consent, caregiver calls, AI interpretation, documentation, and translated home instructions.
body_markdown:
###


Ask students and caregivers separately, recording each person's preferred spoken language, dialect, written language, and communication needs. A single shared field can mask different proficiency levels, particularly when a student speaks English at school but a caregiver does not.


###


Opalite Health's phone workflow calls the provider's number directly from the web portal, removing the manual call-merging step that slows down unplanned caregiver calls. On-demand human interpreters remain a good option for patient preference or unresolved concerns, but for routine caregiver calls across a lean school clinic team, clinically tested AI with automated quality safeguards is a faster, lower-cost first-line choice.


###


Teach-back asks students or caregivers to explain the care plan in their own words, so you can spot gaps in understanding instead of assuming a translated instruction was clear. When an answer reveals confusion, rephrase that specific instruction and check again before closing the visit.


###


Test realistic medication conversations in each pilot language, covering drug names, doses, units, timing, and negations such as "do not take," before expanding a workflow. Combine automated quality checks with caregiver teach-back to confirm the interpreted meaning matches the source, and document any errors or unresolved concerns against your quality thresholds.


###


Pilot one clinic workflow first and track connection time, completed caregiver calls, understanding checks, interpretation concerns, staff effort, and total cost per interpreted encounter. Set clear thresholds for timely access, acceptable cost, and communication quality; separate results by language and workflow before expanding.
